content: In a laboratory setting, a lateral flow urine lipoarabinomannan (LF-LAM) test was performed immediately and yielded a positive result. A sample was subsequently sent to the laboratory for moderate-complexity automated nucleic acid amplification testing (MC-aNAAT), which confirmed the presence of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb). The test indicated susceptibility to rifampicin (RIF) but resistance to isoniazid (INH). Due to the detected INH resistance, further investigation was conducted using a genotypic drug susceptibility test (DST) and a second-line line probe assay (SL-LPA), both of which were available in the laboratory. Consequently, the treatment regimen was adjusted to an individualized plan. An additional sample was collected and sent to the national reference laboratory for phenotypic DST. In a high tuberculosis (TB)/HIV prevalence setting, a presumptive TB patient was tested using the Xpert MTB/RIF assay, which detected rifampicin-susceptible TB. First-line TB treatment was initiated. However, due to the high prevalence of isoniazid-resistant TB (Hr-TB) in the region, further testing for INH resistance was conducted using a low-complexity automated NAAT (LC-aNAAT). This test confirmed INH resistance but showed susceptibility to fluoroquinolones. The treatment was modified to an Hr-TB regimen with the addition of levofloxacin. In another scenario, a patient in an urban clinic with high rifampicin resistance prevalence was diagnosed with multidrug-resistant TB (MDR-TB) using an MC-aNAAT. A second sample was tested with an LC-aNAAT, which confirmed resistance to both INH and FQ. The patient was referred to a specialized center for individualized treatment. Additional genotypic and phenotypic DST testing revealed pyrazinamide (PZA) resistance using a high-complexity reverse hybridization NAAT (HC-rNAAT). The treatment regimen was adjusted based on the resistance pattern. These examples highlight the importance of diagnostic tools like MC-aNAAT, which can simultaneously detect INH and RIF resistance at the initial TB diagnosis. They also emphasize the need to consider local epidemiological contexts, such as high Hr-TB or MDR-TB prevalence, to guide testing and treatment decisions. Centralized models with sample referral networks are critical in addressing patient needs, particularly in settings with limited resources. The implementation of new diagnostic algorithms requires formal evaluation, review, and approval by national health authorities, including the Ministry of Health (MoH), National TB Program (NTP), and National TB Reference Laboratory (NTRL). These processes often involve thematic working groups comprising local officials, implementing partners, civil society, and laboratory and medical professionals. Key considerations include the diagnostic tests in use, WHO recommendations, specimen collection and transport systems, laboratory capacity, and the characteristics of the population being served. The WHO operational handbook on TB diagnostics provides detailed guidance on the use of molecular assays, such as the Xpert MTB/RIF and Xpert MTB/XDR, for detecting TB and drug resistance. These assays are recommended for use on respiratory samples to detect pulmonary TB and resistance to RIF and INH, offering a faster alternative to culture-based DST. However, their performance on non-sputum samples and in extrapulmonary TB cases remains limited. The handbook also outlines the importance of integrating TB testing into multi-disease platforms to optimize resources and improve access to diagnostics. In summary, the examples and guidelines underscore the critical role of advanced diagnostic tools and tailored algorithms in managing TB and DR-TB, particularly in high-burden settings.
